Equine-assisted therapy

A horse responds to what your nervous system is actually doing, not to what you are presenting. That is the whole reason this works. Equine-assisted sessions with Reem Glasco, LPC-S, run near Dripping Springs, about forty minutes from Austin, for adults 18 and over, after a free consult and one to three online sessions. There is no riding. You are on the ground, and most of what happens is noticing.

What a horse notices

Prey animals survive by reading intention and arousal faster and more accurately than we do. A horse will move away from someone who is saying all the right things while holding their breath, and settle next to someone who has genuinely arrived. It is not mystical. It is a very good sensor pointed at exactly the thing therapy usually has to infer from words.

That makes horses an unusually direct teacher of presence, and an unusually honest mirror for the gap between what you intend and what you are actually doing. People who have spent years being competent at therapy often meet something here they have been able to talk their way around indoors.

The horse is Blu. He is not a prop and he is not trained to perform anything therapeutic; he simply responds to whoever is standing in front of him, which is the entire point.

What happens in a session

  • Arriving, and noticing what your body does on the way in.
  • Being near the horse, without a task, longer than feels comfortable.
  • Simple ground work: approaching, leading, stopping, asking.
  • Talking about what just happened, which is where the therapy lives.

Why online sessions come first

One to three online sessions before the first equine session is not a formality. It establishes pacing, gives you a way to settle that you have already practiced, and means neither of us is meeting the other for the first time in a field. The same requirement applies to trail walk sessions.

Who it suits

People who talk more easily when something else is happening. People whose self-awareness is strong in words and thin in the body. People working on boundaries, because asking a thousand-pound animal to move is boundaries with the abstraction removed.

Who it does not

Anyone under 18, anyone with a horse allergy, and anyone currently in crisis, for whom stabilization online comes first. If you are frightened of horses, that is worth discussing rather than ruling yourself out: fear is workable material, but it should be chosen rather than endured.

Questions about equine therapy

Do I ride the horse?

No. All of the work is on the ground. This is equine-assisted psychotherapy, not therapeutic riding, and no riding experience is needed or wanted.

Where do the equine sessions happen?

Near Dripping Springs, Texas, roughly forty minutes from central Austin. The specific location is arranged with you once the online sessions are done.

Who is the horse?

Blu, a bay gelding, near Dripping Springs. You work with him on the ground. He has no routine to run through and nothing to demonstrate; what he does is respond to your state, which is what makes the session useful.

Do I need experience with horses?

None at all. Most people arrive with no horse experience, and the session is built around noticing rather than skill. Being nervous around horses is workable material, not a disqualification, but it should be something you choose to walk toward.

Can I start with an equine session?

No. Equine, trail walk and movement sessions all begin after a free consult and one to three online sessions, so the pacing and the working relationship are established before the setting changes.

Is equine therapy available for teenagers?

No. These sessions are for adults 18 and over. The practice does not work with young children and does not offer in-person sessions to anyone under 18.

Do you offer equine work for therapists rather than clients?

Yes, and it is a separate offering. LPC Associates supervised by Reem can add equine supervision sessions at $60 each, and training for therapists who want to work with horses themselves is available through retreats and training.
